sections.overview: The beech marten is a medium-sized mustelid with a long, supple body, short legs and a bushy tail. Its native range spans much of Europe and central Asia east to the Himalaya and north-west China. It uses woodland, rocky slopes and settled landscapes, and in parts of Europe regularly shelters in buildings. The species is also called the stone marten. An introduced population has been reported in southeastern Wisconsin, outside its native range; this isolated record should not be confused with the native American marten, a different species.
sections.identification: Adults generally have sandy to dark brown fur, a cream-white throat and chest patch, rounded ears and a long tail; the head is elongated and angular. The pale bib often forks and may extend down the forelegs. The fur on the underside of the paws is sparse, a useful close-view distinction from the Eurasian pine marten. That relative, Martes martes, usually has a smaller yellowish or cream bib, larger ears and furrier feet. The beech marten’s pinkish-brown nose contrasts with the darker nose of Martes martes. Adults typically measure 45–60 cm head–body, with a 25–30 cm tail, and weigh 1.2–2.3 kg.
sections.habitat: Across its range the species occupies deciduous woodland, scrub, forest edges, open rocky ground and farmland. In southern Portugal, radio-tracked martens used structurally complex cork-oak woodland together with riparian strips, orchards and pasture; foraging and resting sites differed by sex and landscape scale. In several central European regions, animals also occupy villages and cities, nesting in attics, barns, garages or wall cavities. Urban tolerance is not universal: the IUCN account reports greater woodland association in Israel. Habitat use therefore reflects local resources and landscape, rather than a simple preference for either forest or people.
sections.diet: The beech marten is an opportunistic omnivore. It takes small mammals, birds and eggs, reptiles, invertebrates and carrion, as well as fruit and other plant material. Stomach analyses in central Greece found animal prey especially prominent in spring, when small vertebrates and arthropods were frequent; fruits and insects became more important in summer and autumn as seasonal foods ripened. The pattern shifted among seasons and individuals, rather than following one fixed menu.
sections.behavior: Beech martens forage mainly at night and spend daylight hours in sheltered resting places. They are generally solitary outside breeding; scent marks signal territorial boundaries. In two towns in Luxembourg, radio-tracked animals held stable territories through the year, mostly within the urban boundary; territories of males and females overlapped little with those of the same sex. Urban living did not erase this spacing pattern. Local food and shelter can bring individuals into human structures, while their routine movements still follow territorial boundaries.
sections.reproduction: Mating occurs in summer, but birth follows the next spring because development pauses after fertilization. A study of more than 100 animals from the Bordeaux region documented about eight months of delayed implantation, ending in late February; implantation is followed by roughly 30 days of active gestation. Litters are born around late March or early April. The young are initially helpless and remain in a den while the mother nurses them. In the Bordeaux study, nursing could continue until mid-May. After weaning, juveniles continue to develop and learn to forage before becoming independent later in the year. The long pause separates mating from the brief period of embryo growth and birth.
sections.ecology: In Bussaco National Forest in central Portugal, a study recovered seeds from stone-marten scats and tested their germination, including seeds of native plants and introduced cherry laurel. Gut passage increased and accelerated germination of native elmleaf blackberry, Rubus ulmifolius, but did not measurably affect cherry laurel; preference for that introduced fruit may nonetheless help it spread. Martens also used orchards, woodland edges and buildings in the southern Portuguese landscape studied by radio-tracking, linking their ecology to cultivated and less-modified patches.
sections.conservation: Published in 2016 from an assessment dated 3 March 2015, the IUCN classified the species as Least Concern globally, citing its broad range, large population and occurrence in protected areas. Persecution and fur hunting occur locally, but assessors found no evidence of widespread decline from these pressures. Jordan’s 2020 national mammal Red Data Book lists the species as Endangered there and cites habitat degradation and direct killing, illustrating how regional circumstances differ.
